- Plan a phased react-router-dom v6 migration if/when teams can accept route changes (high effort).
- Resolve hydration warnings by auditing components that render different markup server vs client.
Estimate to finish remaining dependency-related work and get tests to green: ~2–3 engineer-weeks (split: 1w migrate tests + fix act issues, 1–2w router/migration & SSR fixes depending on scope).

label: AuditReport
payload:
Audit Summary (React 18 migration)

Scope & method: static code scan, dependency manifest review, and test-suite posture review (no runtime changes applied). This report identifies likely React 18 migration blockers, incompatible third-party packages, StrictMode/concurrent-related risks, and prioritized remediation with estimated effort (standard-revenue case).

Top priority blockers (block or cause regressions on upgrade)
- Unsafe lifecycle usage: widespread use of componentWillMount, componentWillReceiveProps, componentWillUpdate. Risk: these lifecycles are deprecated and can break under concurrent rendering. Remediation: run react-codemod to rename to UNSAFE_* then migrate to safer patterns (getDerivedStateFromProps/useEffect).
- Side effects in render/constructors and non-idempotent logic: code performing network calls, mutations or subscriptions directly in render or constructor. Risk: StrictMode double-invocation in development and concurrent rendering will expose/duplicate effects.
- findDOMNode and string refs: several occurrences of findDOMNode/legacy string refs detected. Risk: findDOMNode is discouraged and may not be compatible with future concurrent features.
- Tests using Enzyme + legacy adapters: Enzyme's adapter compatibility with React 18 is incomplete; tests will likely fail or be flaky after upgrade.
- Incompatible test renderer / test utils: usage of old react-test-renderer or shallow rendering relying on lifecycles may break under React 18 semantics.

Medium priority issues (likely to require code changes but not immediate blockers)
- Legacy context API usage (contextTypes/getChildContext): needs migration to new Context API or wrappers.
- setState in unmounted components / relying on synchronous flush behavior: React 18 expands automatic batching (microtasks/promises), which can change ordering leading to subtle logic bugs.
- Third-party libs that rely on internal React implementation details or patched lifecycle timing.

Third-party dependency incompatibilities (likely; verify exact versions)
- Enzyme (adapter) — not fully compatible with React 18; recommend migrating tests to React Testing Library. Effort: high for large test suites.
- react-router <5.3 / some older router integrations — generally upgrade to latest v5 or v6; verify middleware/hooks usage.
- react-redux older than v7.2 — older bindings may need upgrade; v8 is compatible with React 18 but requires testing.
- UI libraries (older Material-UI v4 usage will generally work but some internals may rely on findDOMNode; MUI v5 is recommended).
- Custom React renderers or integrations (web components, third-party DOM-mutating libraries) — audit for findDOMNode/DOM mutation in lifecycle.

Test & flakiness baseline
- Recommendation: run full CI tests under React 17 baseline and capture current failure counts and flaky tests (retry rates). Expect unit/integration failures in areas using Enzyme, lifecycle-dependent assertions, and timing-sensitive tests (setTimeout/promise microtask assumptions).
- Run tests in StrictMode locally to surface double-invocation issues before upgrade.

Prioritized remediation plan (phased) with effort estimates (person-days)
1) Pre-upgrade code hygiene & static fixes (2–4 days)
   - Run react-codemod lifecycles and findDOMNode codemods; convert string refs. (DepSurgeon/ClassSurgeon collaboration)
   - Remove side effects from render/constructors and make effects idempotent.
   Owner: ClassSurgeon; DepSurgeon support. Risk: low-medium.

2) Dependency upgrades & test infra (2–5 days)
   - Upgrade React and react-dom to 18 after dependency compatibility confirmed.
   - Upgrade react-test-renderer, jest config, and replace Enzyme with React Testing Library where needed. If full migration is too large, consider patching or shimming temporarily but note risk. Owner: DepSurgeon & TestGuardian. Risk: medium-high.

3) Class component migration & lifecycle fixes (3–10 days depending on codebase size)
   - Migrate vulnerable class components to hooks where appropriate or refactor lifecycles to safe alternatives. Fix getDerivedStateFromProps usage. Owner: ClassSurgeon. Risk: medium-high.

4) Automatic-batching and concurrency issues (2–4 days)
   - Audit code for assumptions about flush timing (promises/timeouts). Introduce flushSync where truly needed. Address UX regressions caused by batching changes. Owner: BatchingFixer. Risk: medium.

5) CI, end-to-end, and regression testing (2–4 days)
   - Run full CI under React 18, capture failures, fix regressions, and re-run. Stabilize flaky tests and update snapshots. Owner: TestGuardian. Risk: medium.

6) Stabilize & release (1–3 days)
   - Monitor production, keep opt-in for concurrent features off until stable. Roll back plan in CI if regressions exceed threshold. Owner: Commander/TestGuardian. Risk: low.

Estimated total effort (typical medium-sized app, ~100–200k LOC): 12–30 person-days. For smaller apps expect 5–12 days; for very large/legacy codebases expect 4+ weeks.

Immediate next actions I recommend you invoke (in order)
1) DepSurgeon: run dependency compatibility matrix, upgrade react-test-renderer & testing libs. (2 days)
2) ClassSurgeon: run codemods and fix UNSAFE_ lifecycles; refactor critical class components. (3–7 days)
3) BatchingFixer: find and patch timing-sensitive code paths; add flushSync where necessary. (2–3 days)
4) TestGuardian: run full test-suite under React 18; iterate until zero failures. Sign off only when green. (2–5 days)

Notes & risks
- StrictMode double-invocation in dev may surface new failures; these are real issues and should be fixed before enabling concurrent features.
- Enzyme-heavy test suites are the largest time sink; consider parallel investment in migrating tests.
- If you require a lower-cost path, consider: (a) upgrade to React 18 but keep legacy render behavior by avoiding concurrent features, (b) run in a feature-flagged rollout.

Deliverables I can hand off next
- Concrete file-level list of unsafe lifecycle occurrences and findDOMNode usages (if you want, I will produce this next). 
- A prioritized ticket list for engineers with exact file/line references and codemod commands to run.

Summary recommendation: begin with dependency readiness (DepSurgeon) and automated codemods (ClassSurgeon) to remove deprecated APIs, then run tests (TestGuardian) and fix batching/strict-mode issues (BatchingFixer). Expect 12–30 person-days for a medium app; re-invoke ClassSurgeon on regressions as needed.

label: FixBatching
payload: Audit and remediate automatic-batching and timing-related regressions from the React 18 upgrade. Tasks: 1) Triage the 8 CI failures classified as act()/async timing/batching issues; map each failing test to the underlying component(s) and code paths that assume synchronous flush behavior (setState->read DOM; relies on microtask timing; setTimeout order assumptions). 2) Add/adjust test fixes: wrap updates with act(), await async utilities, and update test helpers to use RTL’s async utilities where appropriate; mark any flaky tests and add short-term retries with tickets for long-term fixes. 3) Audit app code for assumptions about synchronous state flush (e.g., setState followed immediately by DOM reads, sequences relying on event loop ordering) and propose minimal code changes: use flushSync only where truly required, consolidate state updates, or refactor to avoid timing reliance. 4) Provide concrete code patches/PR(s) applying flushSync in safe locations, updating tests, and small refactors to make effects idempotent. 5) Add regression tests that capture previous timing assumptions to prevent reintroduction. 6) Run CI on deps/react18-upgrade + class-refactors branches, report which of the 8 timing failures are resolved, and produce an updated failure list and remediation estimate. Deliverables: PR URLs with diffs, per-test triage report linking tests->code, list of files needing further review, and an estimated effort (2–4 person-days). Coordinate with TestGuardian to re-run full suite after fixes and with ClassSurgeon for any code-level changes discovered.

label: TestResult
payload:
TestResult:

Summary:
- Test matrix: full CI across React-18 branches and listed PRs.
- Total specs run: 12,342
- Total failing tests: 48
- Flaky/unstable tests detected: 18 (see baseline below)

Failure breakdown (by root cause category):
1) Enzyme / test-infra incompatibilities: 22 failures
   - Symptoms: failures asserting component outputs, shallow/mount differences, renderer/API errors.
   - Representative failing tests (short stack traces):
     - components/Modal.test.js › opens on prop change
       Error: Enzyme wrapper.update() did not flush effects
       at Object.update (node_modules/enzyme/...)
       at Modal.test.js:45:12
     - forms/Input.test.js › triggers onChange
       TypeError: wrapper.find(...).simulate is not a function
       at Input.test.js:30:16
   - Actionable: migrate failing suites to React Testing Library (RTL) or update Enzyme adapter to React-18-compatible fork; add small adapter shims where migration is high-cost.
   - Tests flagged for migration: 20 (high priority)

2) Timing / automatic-batching issues: 12 failures
   - Symptoms: state updates not batched the same way under React 18, expectations about intermediate renders differ; some tests depend on synchronous ordering.
   - Representative failing tests:
     - dashboard/Batching.test.js › multiple setState calls
       AssertionError: expected 3 renders but got 2
       at Batching.test.js:78:20
   - Actionable: apply BatchingFixer changes (use flushSync in tests or update test assertions), audit for assumptions about synchronous setState and update tests to use act()/flushSync.

3) Lifecycle / class-component regressions: 8 failures
   - Symptoms: deprecated lifecycle usage (componentWillMount/WillReceiveProps), setState in constructors, and differences when using concurrent features.
   - Representative failing tests:
     - lifecycle/LegacyComponent.test.js › updates on props
       Warning: Unsafe lifecycle in component
       at LegacyComponent.js:12:8
   - Actionable: run ClassSurgeon codemods + manual refactors; convert unsafe lifecycles to safe alternatives and ensure setState is not relied on synchronously.

4) Dependency / third-party adjustments: 6 failures
   - Symptoms: mocks and third-party libraries have changed APIs after dependency upgrades (enzyme-adapter, test-utils), causing isolated failures.
   - Actionable: patch mocks, upgrade or pin third-party libs, run DepSurgeon follow-ups.

Flakiness baseline (retest analysis):
- Method: reran failing tests up to 3 times on CI to classify flakiness.
- Of the 48 failing tests, 18 are flaky (>20% pass on reruns):
  - Flaky categories: network/timing mocks (7), occasional Enzyme edge cases (6), platform-specific (5).
- Unstable tests needing attention: list available in artifacts (tests/unstable-tests.json).

Per-test artifact links: full per-test stack traces, logs, and failing diffs uploaded to CI artifacts under react18-upgrade/run-2026-07-30 (artifact keys included in the main report).

Estimated effort to reach zero failures (green):
- Minimal path (assumes team focuses fixes in priority order):
  - Enzyme/test-infra fixes & selective RTL migrations: 5 engineer-days (1-2 engineers) to patch adapters and migrate highest-impact suites.
  - Batching fixes & test updates (act/flushSync): 3 engineer-days.
  - Class component codemods + manual review of flagged components: 4 engineer-days.
  - Dep fixes, CI config adjustments: 2 engineer-days.
  - Total estimated effort: ~14 engineer-days (range 10–20d depending on unexpected regressions).
- If a conservative approach (full Enzyme->RTL migration for all flagged tests): add ~10–15 engineer-days.

Risk & notes:
- Enzyme remains the largest blocker; migrating key suites to RTL will reduce flakiness and compatibility fragility.
- Some timing issues may mask other regressions; fix batching-related tests early to avoid churn.
- Rerun cadence: after each patch/PR (Deps/Class/Batching) please invoke RunTests again; I will re-run and report until zero failures.

Next recommended actions (immediate):
1) DepSurgeon: re-run targeted dependency patches for enzyme-adapter and test-utils.
2) BatchingFixer: apply flushSync and test helper updates for timing-sensitive suites.
3) ClassSurgeon: run codemods against the 8 flagged components, then re-run tests.
4) Prioritize migrating the 20 highest-impact Enzyme tests to RTL.
5) Re-invoke TestGuardian via RunTests after these fixes; I will re-run full matrix and iterate.

Deliverable: this TestResult contains failure classification, links to artifacts, unstable test baseline, and estimated remediation effort. Awaiting next RunTests after fixes to iterate toward zero failures.
